registers.name_in_paper: registry data on equal-split after-tax labor income
registers.role: calibration of the labor income process (age fixed effects, demographic controls, variance decomposition)

registers.name_in_paper: Danish registry data (benchmark sample) on cohort size by year

registers.name_in_paper: register data on pension benefits of retirees

linkages: Several Statistics Denmark datasets merged into an annual longitudinal household panel with wealth, earnings and household composition (p. 8).
Assets owned by each household member aggregated to the household and split equally between adult members (normalized/equal-split measure) (p. 9).
Household-head characteristics (e.g. age) attributed to the entire household; head defined as the man in mixed-sex households (p. 9).

sample.universe: all Danish households (normalized equal-split adult individuals), individuals above twenty years of age, excluding those above that age who live with their parents
sample.unit_of_observation: normalized (equal-split) household = adult individual, observed annually
selection_rules: individuals above twenty years of age
exclude those above twenty who live with their parents
exclude self-employed people (they do not pay into the mandatory pension scheme)
exclude households with more than two adult members
in Fig. 5, restrict to households whose head is younger than 100 years
the 60-69 subsample conditions on the household head being in the 60-69 age group

construction_notes: Net wealth = real and financial assets (incl. pension assets net of taxes, excl. consumer durables such as cars) minus liabilities (p. 9).
Wealth measured at the normalized (equal-split) household level; household wealth divided between adult members (p. 9).
Monetary amounts in constant 2015 DKK; model monetary values in thousands of 2015 DKK (p. 9, Tables 2-3).

Pension assets before 2014 imputed by modifying Jakobsen et al. (2020): aggregate private pension assets attributed to individuals by their share of income and contributions to private pensions (p. 10).
Hodrick-Prescott filter with lambda = 300 applied to the annual inequality series in Figs. 1 and 13; lambda = 100 for the data series in Fig. 8.
The 'median' household graph in Fig. 5 is based on the average asset and debt holdings of 100 households in a given age group with net wealth closest to the median (footnote 13, p. 9).
Extended wealth = net wealth + imputed PAYG wealth, where PAYG wealth is the NPV of future PAYG benefits net of implicit contributions, following Catherine et al. (2020) (p. 20).

Implicit PAYG contributions assumed proportional to total income taxes paid, under a balanced government budget; life-cycle earnings paths for working-age individuals taken from simulations of the calibrated model (p. 20).

The calibrated life-cycle model is solved by the endogenous gridpoint method and simulated annually between the 1970 and 2100 steady states, with 22 million independent draws of income shocks (pp. 11, 14).
The discount-factor distribution is approximated by a seven-point equidistant grid [b-3d, ..., b+3d] with b = 0.954 and d = 0.0117, i.e. beta in [0.9189, 0.9891] (p. 14, Table 2).

claims.statement: Between 1992 and 2017, over the transition of the Danish pension system towards a dominant fully-funded pillar, the Gini coefficient of net wealth among all Danish households fell by -8%.

treatment.label: Transition of the Danish pension system from mainly PAYG to a hybrid with a dominant fully-funded pillar, 1992 vs. 2017

definition.value: Calendar contrast between 1992 — the pre-transition benchmark year, chosen because private-sector contribution rates started to increase from 1993 — and 2017, the last sample year, by which contribution rates had reached their permanent level (from close to zero in 1992 to about 12 to 15 percent in most occupations by 2009). Contribution rates apply to DI/CO collective agreements (Fig. 2).

timing.value: contrast between the 1992 and the 2017 cross-section

outcome.label: Gini coefficient of net wealth, all households

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark database on households' assets and liabilities (2014-2017); earlier years from a previous Statistics Denmark wealth dataset with imputed pension assets. No register code or variable name is given in the main text (Appendix C)

definition.value: Gini coefficient of net wealth, i.e. real and financial assets (encompassing pension assets net of taxes but not consumer durables such as cars) minus liabilities, measured at the normalized (equal-split) household level; private pension assets are observed from 2014 and imputed for earlier years

timing.value: cross-section of 1992 and of 2017

units.value: percent change in the inequality measure between 1992 and 2017, as printed in Table 1

estimand.target_population: Danish households (equal-split adult individuals) in the benchmark register sample
estimand.time_horizon: change between 1992 and 2017 (25 years)

population.description: Danish households, measured as normalized (equal-split) adult individuals, from merged Statistics Denmark registers; individuals above twenty years of age excluding those living with their parents, excluding self-employed people and households with more than two adult members
population.ages: above 20 (household head younger than 100 in the cross-sectional figures)
subgroups_defined: ten-year age bins of the household head
population.selection: self-employed people are excluded because they do not pay into the mandatory pension scheme; households with more than two adults are excluded because wealth items cannot be attributed; individuals above twenty living with their parents are excluded

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the same inequality statistic is compared across Danish administrative register cross-sections, 1992 (the pre-transition benchmark year, chosen because private-sector contribution rates started rising in 1993) versus 2017 (the last sample year, by which contribution rates had reached their permanent level). The paper describes the decline as accompanying the pension transition; the attribution to the reform is made with the calibrated model in Section 5.3.

key_assumptions.assumption: Private pension assets are observed only from 2014; for earlier years aggregate private pension assets are attributed to individuals by their share of income and contributions to private pensions (a modification of Jakobsen et al., 2020), and the imputation is assumed to reproduce the distribution of pension wealth
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnote 16 (p. 10): Figure C.6 in Appendix C.3 shows the overlap of the imputed series with the 2014-2017 data, and the imputation is said to match the aggregate wealth shares held by specific wealth deciles quite well

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on not being self-employed, on having at most two adult members, and on being above age twenty and not living with parents
key_assumptions.supported_by: footnotes 11, 12 and 18: conclusions are stated to be unchanged when self-employed households or households with more than two adults are included and when the household head is defined as the primary earner (Appendix C.4; Andersen et al., 2022)

implies_edges.from: self-employment or more than two adults in household
implies_edges.to: sample inclusion

key_assumptions.assumption: The 1992-2017 comparison is descriptive: the paper claims only that the decline in wealth inequality accompanied the transition to a more funded pension system and does not identify an effect of the reform from this comparison
key_assumptions.supported_by: the causal decomposition is carried out only in the counterfactual simulations of Table 4

key_assumptions.assumption: Household wealth is split equally between the adult members of the household (normalized / equal-split measure) and head characteristics are attributed to the whole household

threats_discussed: pension assets are not observed before 2014 and must be imputed
the sample excludes self-employed households and households with more than two adults
the Gini coefficient across all age groups partly reflects that age groups are at different phases of the life cycle
the Gini coefficient is sensitive to the tails of the distribution
robustness_checks: imputed pension-asset series compared with the 2014-2017 register data (Figure C.6, footnote 16)
top 1% and top 0.1% wealth shares over time (Figures C.7 and C.8, footnote 17)
including self-employed households (Appendix C.4; Andersen et al., 2022; footnotes 17-18)
including households with more than two adult members (footnote 12)
defining the household head as the primary earner rather than as the man in mixed-sex households (footnote 11)
households without children, to check for a bequest motive (Figure C.4, footnote 14)
four alternative inequality measures reported side by side in Table 1
unresolved_confounders: the descriptive comparison does not separate the pension transition from other time-varying factors; the paper notes that part of the decline in the model is driven by aggregate income growth and that remaining data movements may reflect macroeconomic fluctuations

estimation.weights: wealth measured at the normalized (equal-split) household level, i.e. household wealth divided between adult members

source_table.value: Table 1, Gini coefficient panel, all households column

heterogeneity.dimension: age group of the household head (all households vs. head 60-69)
heterogeneity.finding: Table 1 reports the decline for all households and, separately, for households with head aged 60-69; the paper states the drop in the Gini coefficient was even more notable, by 18%, for households near retirement

claims.statement: In the calibrated life-cycle model, the Danish pension reform (full model) implies a change of -8.9 percentage points in the wealth Gini coefficient between 1992 and 2017 for 60-69 year olds.

treatment.label: The Danish pension reform as modelled (full model): the trend increase in the mandated fully-funded pension contribution rate from its 1992 value of 5.2%, together with the income-dependent contribution component and the endogenous decline in effective PAYG generosity, along the baseline transition path

register_source.value: contribution rates calibrated to the benchmark register sample; PAYG replacement rates from Finansministeriet (2017b)

definition.value: Policy path of the pension system in the simulated transition. The reform is parameterised by pi_{i,n} = pi_bar + pi(Y_{i,n}); between 1992 and 2009 the average contribution rate in the data increases from 5.2% to 10.9% and contribution rates are restricted to [0, 0.18].

timing.value: the baseline (full model) transition path from 1992 to 2017

outcome.label: percentage-point change in the model-simulated Gini coefficient of wealth between 1992 and 2017, 60-69 year olds

register_source.value: model output; the targets and comparison moments come from the Danish administrative register benchmark sample

definition.value: Gini coefficient of (net) wealth in the simulated cross-section of 2017 minus that of 1992, in percentage points, computed over simulated agents weighted by actual cohort sizes; wealth is voluntary assets plus funded pension assets

timing.value: difference between the simulated 2017 and 1992 cross-sections

units.value: percentage points of the Gini coefficient, change 1992 to 2017

magnitude.interpretation: a decline of almost ten percentage points in the Gini coefficient of the 60-69 year olds, close to the data decline

estimand.target_population: simulated agents of the calibrated Danish life-cycle model aged 60-69; the object is a distributional statistic, not an individual-level treatment effect
estimand.time_horizon: change between 1992 and 2017 (25 years) along the simulated transition
estimand.formal_query: Gini(wealth)_2017 - Gini(wealth)_1992 under the baseline path

population.description: Simulated agents in the calibrated overlapping-generations life-cycle model of the Danish economy (ages 20-99, retirement at 65), weighted by the actual cohort size by year from the Danish registry benchmark sample
population.birth_cohorts: cohorts alive along the simulated 1970-2100 transition path
population.period: annual simulations between the 1970 and 2100 steady states; reported for 1992 and 2017
population.selection: the model is calibrated to the same benchmark register sample (equal-split households, self-employed and households with more than two adults excluded)

identification.source_of_variation: Simulated policy variation inside a calibrated overlapping-generations life-cycle model of the Danish economy: the trend increase in mandated fully-funded (occupational) pension contribution rates along the annual transition path between the 1970 and 2100 steady states. Counterfactual worlds mute single reform elements from 1992 onward: (b) no trend in pi_bar, (c) no income-dependent contributions, (d) no change in the PAYG rate.

key_assumptions.assumption: The model is calibrated to 1992 (the year before the reform): the midpoint and dispersion of the discount-factor distribution are chosen to match the Gini coefficient of the 60-69 year olds and the peak of non-pension cross-sectional assets, and the income-dependent contribution rate is set to match peak FF pension assets in 1992
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports the fit on targeted and on untargeted 1992 and 2017 moments
